mainEntity.name: How much does restumping cost in Ballarat?

acceptedAnswer.text: Restumping in the Ballarat area typically runs about $400–$700 per stump. A smaller weatherboard home with around 50 stumps often lands near $8,000–$9,000, while larger homes with 100 or more stumps can exceed $16,000. Levelling floors or replacing damaged bearers and joists adds to the total. We would rather inspect the subfloor than quote from a photograph, because stump count, underfloor clearance and access are what actually move the price.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my Ballarat home needs restumping?

acceptedAnswer.text: The common signs are sloping or bouncy floors, doors and windows that stick, cracks in plaster or cornices, and gaps opening between walls and skirting boards. None of these prove the stumps have failed on their own — movement can have more than one cause — but together they are worth investigating. Older homes still on original timber stumps are most at risk in the region's cold, damp conditions, where the timber typically fails at ground level.

mainEntity.name: Do I need a building permit to restump a house in Victoria?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Restumping, also called reblocking, is building work in Victoria and requires a building permit issued through a registered building surveyor. The permit brings mandatory inspection points with it, including an inspection before the new stumps are covered. We arrange the permit and the inspections as part of the job.

mainEntity.name: Do you charge to come out and quote?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Assessing the subfloor and quoting the work is free and carries no obligation. We look at stump condition, bearers, joists and access, take floor levels, and explain what we find in plain terms before setting out a written scope.

mainEntity.name: Can restumping fix my sloping floors completely?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can usually improve them substantially, but a perfectly flat result is rarely realistic on an older home. A house that has settled over decades has taken up that shape through its frame, linings and joinery. We measure the floor with a laser level, tell you what degree of correction is practical for your building, and lift progressively so the structure has time to take up the change.

mainEntity.name: How long does restumping take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A small partial reblocking job is often a few days. A full house restump generally runs one to two weeks, depending on stump count, underfloor access and what the excavation turns up. Ballarat winters can stretch that out — saturated ground is slower to dig and concrete takes longer to cure in the cold.

WHAT SETS US APART

Why Ballarat homeowners call us
Local building knowledge

Ballarat's housing stock runs from goldfields-era weatherboards to brick veneers of the seventies and new estates in Lucas and Winter Valley, and they fail in different ways. A cottage in Soldiers Hill on original timber stumps has a different problem from a settled slab in Alfredton. We inspect the building in front of us and explain what its particular construction and age mean for the work.

We measure before we quote

A restumping scope built from what is visible at the street is a guess. We get under the house where access allows, check stump condition, bearers, joists, ventilation and drainage, and take floor levels with a laser so the extent of movement is a number rather than an impression. That is what makes the quote hold once work starts.

Clear scope and pricing

Foundation work is hard to budget for when the underlying problem is vague. We set out the areas being addressed, the stump count, the access considerations and what is excluded, in language you can actually compare against another quote. Questions before work starts are welcome — that is when they are cheapest to answer.

Careful, progressive levelling

Lifting a house is done in stages, with levels rechecked as the load moves onto the new stumps. That matters most in Ballarat's older timber homes, where a frame that settled over a century will crack if it is forced back to flat in one movement. We aim for sound, even support and a realistic improvement in level rather than an unachievable promise.

Permits handled properly

Reblocking is building work in Victoria and needs a building permit through a registered building surveyor, with mandatory inspections including one before the new stumps are covered. We arrange the permit and the inspection points as part of the job, so the work is documented — which matters at sale time as much as it does now.

Straightforward communication

Once the floor is up, older houses reveal things nobody could see beforehand — a rotted bearer end, a previous repair, a footing that is not where the plan suggested. When that happens we tell you what we have found and what it means for scope and timing, before we carry on rather than afterwards.

GETTING STARTED

Our restumping process

A straightforward path from first enquiry to finished work, planned around your property and the level of work involved.

Tell us what you've noticed

Start with the symptoms — the sloping room, the door that stopped closing, the crack that keeps coming back. We will ask about the age of the house, any additions, and whether the stumps have ever been done before, which usually tells us a good deal before we arrive.

02
We inspect and take levels

We get under the house where access allows and assess stump condition, bearers, joists, drainage and ventilation, then run a laser survey to record floor heights across every room. You get the findings in plain terms, including the parts that turn out not to need work.

03
You get a written scope

The quote sets out the stump count, the areas being addressed, the material, the permit, and the access considerations that affect the job. It is written so you can compare it line by line against anyone else's, and there is no obligation to proceed.

04
We do the work and sign it off

The floor is supported, stumps replaced on new footings, and levels brought up progressively with checks between stages. At the end we walk the job with you, confirm the levels achieved and hand over the permit documentation.

Ballarat's restumping and reblocking specialists

Ballarat Restumping Kings works on one part of a house: the support underneath it. Uneven floors, doors that have started to bind, tired timber stumps, and the general uncertainty that comes with an ageing subfloor — that is the whole of what we do, and doing one thing means we have seen most of the ways it goes wrong in this city.

We work the way we do because too many people are left in the dark when they notice a crack or a sloping room. A proper look underneath and a straight conversation changes that before any money is committed. SERVICE AREA

Restumping across Ballarat and the Central Highlands

Ballarat is not a city of identical houses, and that is exactly why restumping needs local judgement. What sits beneath a goldfields-era cottage is a different problem from a seventies brick veneer or a recent build on a cut-and-fill block.

In Ballarat Central, Soldiers Hill and Black Hill, a great many streets are Victorian and Edwardian weatherboards that have been renovated, extended and left to settle for a century or more. A floor that has changed shape over that time can be down to ageing stumps, but just as often it involves altered drainage, blocked subfloor ventilation, or changes made during earlier work that nobody documented. We look past the symptom to the condition of the support system as a whole.

Around Alfredton, Lucas and Winter Valley the housing is newer and the questions are different. Block sizes, construction periods and site layouts vary widely, and cut-and-fill on a sloping block can leave one part of a house on very different ground from another. Rather than treating a crack or an uneven room as an automatic diagnosis, we inspect the accessible structure and set out what is actually happening — which is what you need if you are weighing up repairs, a renovation or a sale.

Near Lake Wendouree, Newington and Lake Gardens, established homes tend to sit alongside mature trees and well-kept gardens, and large trees close to a house are a genuine factor in foundation movement on reactive ground. Access planning matters here too. We talk through entry points, underfloor clearance and the route for machinery and spoil before work begins, so the site can be managed without wrecking what is around it.

Ballarat East, Brown Hill and Eureka carry the city's early history through their older residential streets toward the Yarrowee corridor. Many of these properties have been altered across generations and no two underfloors are alike. We assess the existing stump layout, the supporting timbers and the movement visible at the time of inspection, then turn that into a scope you can follow without decoding trade jargon.

In Sebastopol, Delacombe and Redan we are often asked whether floors, sticking doors or plaster cracks mean restumping is needed right now. The honest answer depends on the cause, extent and location of the movement. We investigate the accessible areas and explain how what you are seeing inside relates to what is supporting it below, which helps you prioritise properly instead of treating the whole thing as a mystery.

Beyond the city we work through Buninyong, about fifteen minutes south, and out toward Creswick, Clunes, Daylesford, Beaufort and Maryborough. Each has its own mix of heritage buildings, ground conditions and access constraints, and a Clunes cottage, a Buninyong family home and a Maryborough period residence can all need quite different thinking beneath the floor. Tell us the property location and what you have noticed, and we will take it from there.

QUALITY STANDARDS

Materials and methods we use

The right material and method depend on the age of the house, its layout, the ground it sits on and how much room there is to work. We choose durable components and work in measured stages to protect the structure while the support beneath it is renewed.

Most restumping work replaces deteriorated or inadequate supports with concrete stumps, set and aligned to the structure above. Concrete is the common choice because it does not rot the way old timber does and gives dependable long-term support when it is installed properly. Galvanised steel adjustable stumps are the alternative: they cost more per stump, but the threaded head means the floor can be corrected later by winding rather than by digging, which is worth having on a house with a known movement history.

The stump itself is only half the job. What carries the load is the footing beneath it, and a stump set on an inadequate footing will move regardless of what it is made of. Holes are excavated to the depth the ground requires, footings poured, and stumps set plumb and packed before any load returns to them. Bearers, packing and fixings all matter in the same way — they disappear from view once the work is done, but they determine how load actually travels through the floor system.

Before lifting any section we assess how the building is behaving, then adjust gradually. That is especially important in established homes around Newington, Redan and Ballarat East, where original floors, later additions, chimneys and internal finishes all respond differently to being moved. Slow, controlled work is the difference between correcting a structural problem and creating a cosmetic one in the plaster above.

Good underfloor work also has to account for moisture. We pay attention to drainage, restricted clearance and blocked or insufficient ventilation, because persistent damp is what shortened the life of the original timber and will do the same to new bearers if nothing changes. The finished result should be orderly beneath the house and a sensible base for everyday living, future maintenance and any renovation you have in mind.

PRICING

What affects the cost of your restumping job

Every house sits differently, so an accurate price starts with seeing the conditions rather than guessing from a photograph. Our estimates are built around the work needed to create dependable support, with the scope explained before you decide anything.

The largest factor is simply the extent of the work. Some homes need a handful of failed stumps addressed; others need a replacement program across the whole subfloor. Stump count, house size, stump spacing, the condition of the existing bearers and whether particular areas have settled all feed into the labour and materials required. In the Ballarat area the per-stump figure generally sits around $400–$700, which is why a fifty-stump weatherboard and a hundred-and-twenty-stump home are such different propositions.

Access changes the number as much as size does. A house with generous underfloor clearance and a clear side path is a very different job from one with a 400mm crawl space, a steep approach, established landscaping to protect, or an extension that has cut the subfloor in two. Where machinery cannot reach, excavation and spoil removal happen by hand, and that is labour. Older homes around central Ballarat also tend to reveal earlier alterations beneath the floor that have to be allowed for honestly rather than discovered later.

Ground conditions and the level of correction wanted also matter. Reactive clay, poor drainage and the need to relevel sections progressively all add to the work. The cheapest quote is not automatically the best value if it leaves out site preparation, adequate footings, controlled lifting or the permit — those omissions do not remove the cost, they just move it to a variation later. Structural support is worth taking a long view on.

The free assessment exists so you can understand the likely work before committing to anything. We will talk through what we can see, outline the recommended approach, and be explicit about what needs closer attention once access is available. Useful things to have ready: the age of the house, where you have noticed cracking or movement, any past alterations, and what you are planning to do with the place. That conversation is what turns a range into a number you can rely on.

TIMELINE

How long restumping projects take in Ballarat

Timing depends on the scale of the support work and what turns up beneath the house. We give you a practical indication once we have assessed access, the condition of the existing stumps and the parts of the structure involved.

A smaller, localised reblocking job is often finished within a few days. A full house-wide replacement generally runs one to two weeks and sometimes longer. The difference comes down to stump count, the floor plan, underfloor clearance and whether sections need gradual relevelling rather than a straight replacement. We plan the sequence so the structural work progresses safely and methodically rather than in a rush at the end.

Weather matters more here than in warmer parts of the state, particularly where excavation and concrete are involved. Ballarat's wet, cold months slow site preparation, saturated ground is harder to dig and needs sensible judgement before work proceeds, and concrete takes longer to reach strength in low temperatures. We also factor in material preparation and the practicalities of an occupied house when we set a start date.

On the day, expect the crew to establish access, re-inspect the working area and protect what needs protecting before anything begins. There will be noise and movement around the perimeter and beneath the floor, and we will keep you posted on what is happening rather than leaving you to guess. If hidden conditions change the planned sequence — and in older houses they sometimes do — we explain the reason and what it means before carrying on.

If you are renovating in Ballarat, Buninyong, Creswick or the surrounding districts, it is worth organising foundation work before new flooring, cabinetry or internal finishes go in. Getting the base right first lets the other trades work from a stable floor and avoids the expensive situation where a brand new kitchen has to come out again to get at what is underneath it.

QUALITY STANDARDS

Materials and methods we use

The right material and method depend on the age of the house, its layout, the ground it sits on and how much room there is to work. We choose durable components and work in measured stages to protect the structure while the support beneath it is renewed.

Most restumping work replaces deteriorated or inadequate supports with concrete stumps, set and aligned to the structure above. Concrete is the common choice because it does not rot the way old timber does and gives dependable long-term support when it is installed properly. Galvanised steel adjustable stumps are the alternative: they cost more per stump, but the threaded head means the floor can be corrected later by winding rather than by digging, which is worth having on a house with a known movement history.

The stump itself is only half the job. What carries the load is the footing beneath it, and a stump set on an inadequate footing will move regardless of what it is made of. Holes are excavated to the depth the ground requires, footings poured, and stumps set plumb and packed before any load returns to them. Bearers, packing and fixings all matter in the same way — they disappear from view once the work is done, but they determine how load actually travels through the floor system.

Before lifting any section we assess how the building is behaving, then adjust gradually. That is especially important in established homes around Newington, Redan and Ballarat East, where original floors, later additions, chimneys and internal finishes all respond differently to being moved. Slow, controlled work is the difference between correcting a structural problem and creating a cosmetic one in the plaster above.

Good underfloor work also has to account for moisture. We pay attention to drainage, restricted clearance and blocked or insufficient ventilation, because persistent damp is what shortened the life of the original timber and will do the same to new bearers if nothing changes. WHAT SETS US APART

Why Townsville homeowners call us
Grab rails go into structure, not into lining

This is the most common dangerous shortcut in access work. A grab rail has to hold a person's entire body weight at the moment they are falling, and plasterboard, tile or cement sheet alone will not do it — the fixing pulls out exactly when it is needed. Rails must be fixed to timber noggings between the studs or to purpose-made backing plates. On an existing wall that means taking the lining off, installing backing and making good. It costs more, it takes longer, and there is no version of this we will skip.

We build to the OT report, not around it

An occupational therapist establishes what the person actually needs the home to do — the transfer space beside a toilet, a shower without a hob, a gradient someone can genuinely self-propel. Our job is to price and build that, and to say clearly when something specified will not work on the site so it can be resolved properly rather than quietly substituted. Where there is no report yet we can still quote work you already know you need, but for anything complex the report makes the whole process faster.

High-set Queenslanders, honestly assessed

Townsville's raised housing is what makes ramps hard here. At 1:14, a 1.2 metre floor height needs about 17 metres of ramp plus landings — more than most blocks have in a straight line. Sometimes a switchback fits. Sometimes a platform lift or moving the accessible entry to a lower rear door is genuinely the better answer, and we would rather tell you that at the quoting stage than build a compliant ramp that consumes the yard and is exhausting to use.

Built for the climate, not the catalogue

Access work in the tropics has to survive the tropics. External ramp surfaces need slip resistance that still performs in the wet season, not just when dry. Steel needs proper corrosion protection, because coastal humidity attacks fixings, welds and base plates — and a ramp corroding at its base plate is a structural failure rather than a cosmetic one. Fixtures and hardware get chosen with that in mind rather than specified from a southern supplier's default.

We will tell you when layout beats building

A surprising share of access problems are solved by where furniture sits, which way a door swings, or removing a built-in cupboard rather than moving a wall. Changing a bathroom door from inward-opening to outward or sliding frequently resolves the whole problem — and it also means the door cannot be blocked by someone who has fallen inside. When the cheap answer works we will say so, even though the expensive answer is the one we would be paid for.

GETTING STARTED

Our NDIS home modifications process

A straightforward path from first enquiry to finished work, planned around your property and the level of work involved.

Not a diagnosis — just what is hard about the house as it stands. Getting in, getting to the bathroom, using the shower, turning a corner.

ABOUT US

Access and home modification work across Townsville

We build home modifications in Townsville — bathrooms, ramps, doorway widening, rails and the whole-of-home changes that let someone move through their own house safely. The work comes from NDIS participants and their families, from occupational therapists and support coordinators, and from older residents who want to stay where they are and need the house to catch up.

Townsville shapes this trade more than people outside it expect. The raised Queenslander housing that gives the city its character is genuinely difficult for ramp access — a metre of floor height needs fourteen metres of ramp before you count landings, and most blocks do not have it in a straight line. The tropical climate is the other factor: external steelwork needs proper corrosion protection in this humidity, and slip resistance has to hold up through a wet season rather than in a showroom.

The part we are least willing to compromise on is structural. Grab rails fixed to plasterboard instead of noggings, shower floors graded by eye, waterproofing rushed — those are the failures that hurt someone later, and they are also invisible in a finished bathroom, which is exactly why they are where a cheap quote comes from. If our price is higher than another, that is the question worth asking both of us.

EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW

NDIS Home Modifications in Townsville, answered
How much do NDIS home modifications cost in Townsville?

It depends on the work. Minor (Category A) modifications like grab rails and ramps are under $10,000; Category B minor works run $10,000–$20,000; and complex or structural changes such as a full accessible bathroom are $20,000 and up and need building approval. When approved in your plan, eligible modifications are funded by the NDIS rather than paid out of pocket.

Do I need an occupational therapist assessment first?

Yes. NDIS home modifications start with an OT assessment — an AHPRA-registered occupational therapist assesses your needs and recommends the works, and complex modifications need a specialist home-modification assessor. We can pass your details to local builders who work alongside OTs.

Can OTs or plan managers request quotes on a participant's behalf?

Yes, and it's often the easiest way to run it. Occupational therapists, support coordinators and plan managers can request a quote directly, and we'll turn it around quickly so it can go into an assessment or report without holding up the plan.

Do you work from an occupational therapist's report?

Yes, and the job is cleaner when there is one. An OT report sets out what the home actually needs to do — transfer space beside the toilet, a shower without a hob, a ramp gradient a wheelchair can genuinely manage — and we scope and price the build against that rather than guessing at it. Where there's no report yet, we can still quote work you already know you need. One thing worth sorting early: whether your funding requires a registered provider depends on how your plan is managed, so confirm that with your plan manager or support coordinator before anything is booked.

OUR PROMISE

What you can expect from us
Nothing structural gets skipped to hit a price

Rail backing, correct shower falls, proper waterproofing and adequate lintels are not the items where a cheaper quote should come from. If our price is higher than another, ask both of us what backing the rails are fixed to and how the shower floor is being graded — the answer is usually the difference.

We say when something will not work

If a specified ramp will not fit the block at a usable gradient, or a bathroom cannot achieve turning space without moving a wall, you will hear it before the quote rather than after the work. That sometimes means telling an OT that a recommendation needs revisiting, which is a normal part of the process and better done early.

The household keeps functioning

People live in these houses while the work happens, and often the person who most needs the bathroom is the one whose bathroom is being rebuilt. We stage the work so there is always something usable, keep dust and disruption contained, and tidy up at the end of each day rather than leaving a site until the job finishes.

WHERE WE WORK

Townsville suburb by suburb

Access work is decided by what the house is, not where it is — and around Townsville the housing type changes markedly from suburb to suburb.

North Ward holds much of the older raised housing, and that makes it the hardest area in Townsville for entry access. A traditional high-set Queenslander can sit well over a metre above ground, which at a usable 1:14 gradient needs seventeen metres of ramp plus landings — more than most inner blocks have available in any direction. Switchback designs solve some of it. Where they do not, a platform lift or moving the accessible entry to a rear or under-house door closer to ground level is often the better outcome, and we will raise that rather than building something technically compliant and practically exhausting.

Kirwan is largely single-storey slab-on-ground housing on flat blocks, which is close to the easiest access situation available. Entry ramps are short or unnecessary, thresholds are low, and level-entry shower conversions are simpler because there is no subfloor to work around. The constraint here is internal rather than external: circulation space inside compact bathrooms and hallways, where the fix is usually a wall or a door swing rather than anything to do with the entry.

Aitkenvale and Annandale sit between those two, with a mix of raised and lowset homes and a good deal of 1970s and 1980s stock. That era brings its own pattern — small bathrooms with the toilet in a separate room, narrow internal doorways, and thresholds between every floor covering. The work here is usually less about the entry and more about the path through the house: getting from a bedroom to a bathroom in a wheelchair often needs two doorways widened and a threshold removed rather than one big change.

Douglas is dominated by the hospital and university precinct, and a share of our work there follows hospital discharge — a house that needs to be made safe on a deadline rather than modified at leisure. Those jobs get staged deliberately: grab rails with proper backing, a handrail at the steps and a temporary modular ramp can be done quickly, while a full level-entry bathroom involves waterproofing and drying time that genuinely cannot be compressed. Telling us the discharge date early changes what we recommend doing first.

HOW IT WORKS

How NDIS home modifications actually get approved and built

The building is the straightforward part. The process around it is what people find confusing, and knowing the shape of it makes the whole thing faster.

Home modifications under the NDIS generally fall into two broad groups, and which one you are in changes how much process is involved. Minor modifications are lower-complexity changes that improve safe access without significant structural work — grab rails, lever tapware, a handrail, a small threshold ramp. More substantial home modifications involve structural change: removing a shower hob and re-grading a floor, widening a load-bearing doorway, building a permanent ramp, reconfiguring a bathroom. The second group requires more assessment, more documentation and usually more waiting, which is worth knowing at the start so the timeline is not a surprise.

The sequence is normally the same. An occupational therapist assesses what the person needs the home to do and documents it — this is the foundation of everything downstream, and it is their professional judgement rather than a builder's. Builder quotes are then obtained against that report, which is where we come in. The quotes and the report go to the NDIA or through the plan manager for approval. Once approved, the work is scheduled and built, and for substantial modifications the OT usually confirms on completion that what was built matches what was recommended.

Two things speed this up more than anything else. The first is an itemised quote. If a quote is a single number, a plan manager cannot match it against the report and an approver cannot see what they are approving — and if funding is granted in stages, an unitemised quote cannot be staged. We break quotes down by element for exactly this reason. The second is flagging conflicts early. If a report specifies something that will not work on the actual site — a ramp gradient the block cannot accommodate, turning space a bathroom cannot achieve without moving a wall — that needs raising before the quote goes in, not after approval, because resolving it afterwards means going back around the loop.

One question we get constantly: whether the builder needs to be a registered NDIS provider. That depends on how the plan is managed rather than on the work itself, and it is genuinely worth confirming with your plan manager or support coordinator before anything is booked. It is a straightforward question with a clear answer for your situation, and it is much better established at the start than discovered at invoicing. We are not in a position to advise on your plan — but we would much rather you ask early than assume.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

Why ramps are hard on a Townsville Queenslander

The single most common disappointment in access work here comes down to arithmetic that nobody does until a builder is standing in the yard.

An accessible ramp is built to a gradient of about 1:14 — one unit of rise for every fourteen of horizontal run. That ratio is not arbitrary. It is roughly the limit at which a person can self-propel a manual wheelchair up a slope without assistance, and steeper ramps become both exhausting to ascend and genuinely dangerous to descend. It also means required length is fixed by the height you are climbing, and nothing about design or materials changes it.

Apply that to Townsville's housing. A lowset home with a 300mm step needs a bit over four metres of ramp — easy on almost any block. A traditional high-set Queenslander with a floor 1.2 metres above ground needs around seventeen metres, and the standard also calls for level landings at intervals along the run and at both ends, adding further length. Very few inner-suburban blocks have seventeen metres of clear run available in a straight line, particularly at the front of the house.

The usual solution is a switchback: the ramp runs, turns on a level landing, and runs back the other way, folding the length into the depth of a yard. Done well this is unobtrusive and works fine. It needs width to turn, though, and on a narrow block it can consume most of a side yard or the entire front garden — which is a real cost to a household even when it is not a financial one.

Where a switchback does not fit, two alternatives deserve serious consideration before anyone compromises the gradient. A platform lift needs a fraction of the footprint and handles a large rise directly, at higher cost and with ongoing maintenance. Or the accessible entry moves: many raised Townsville homes have a rear door, a laundry or an under-house area considerably closer to ground level than the front door, and a short ramp there can be far better than a long one at the front. What should not happen is building at 1:8 because that is what fits — a gradient nobody can self-propel is not access, it is a slope with handrails, and it will not pass an OT's review either.

HOW LONG IT TAKES

Why home modifications take longer than the building work does

Almost all of the elapsed time in a modification project happens before anyone picks up a tool — and knowing that changes how you plan it.

The construction itself is usually the shortest phase. A set of properly backed grab rails is a day. A ramp is days to a week or two depending on length and footings. Even a full level-entry bathroom conversion is measured in weeks, and much of that is waterproofing and tiling that has to cure and cannot be hurried — a bathroom rushed at that stage is one that leaks into the wall cavity later.

What takes the time is everything around it. Getting an occupational therapy assessment scheduled and the report written. Obtaining builder quotes, which requires builders to visit, measure and price. Approval, which for substantial modifications is not immediate. And then scheduling the work into a builder's calendar. Each step is reasonable on its own and they add up to months rather than weeks, particularly for structural work.

There are ways to lose less time. Getting quotes organised promptly once the OT report exists is the obvious one — reports sometimes sit while everyone waits for someone else to act. Itemised quotes prevent a round trip when an approver wants to see the breakdown. Raising site conflicts before submission avoids the worst delay of all, which is approval for something that then turns out to be unbuildable as specified. And if the modification is for a rental, landlord consent should be started early rather than at the end, because it is frequently the item that holds everything up and it is entirely outside both our control and the NDIA's.

Where there is a hard deadline — a hospital discharge is the common one — the sensible approach is to split the work. The high-impact, low-complexity items can genuinely be done quickly: rails with proper backing, a handrail at the entry steps, lever hardware, a temporary modular ramp that can be removed later. The structural work is then planned properly on its own timeline. That is a better outcome than compressing a bathroom conversion into a week and living with the consequences, and it is how we would suggest running it if the dates are tight.

Minor (Category A) modifications like grab rails and ramps are under $10,000; Category B minor works run $10,000–$20,000; and complex or structural changes such as a full accessible bathroom are $20,000 and up and need building approval. When approved in your plan, eligible modifications are funded by the NDIS rather than paid out of pocket.

Do I need an occupational therapist assessment first?

Yes. NDIS home modifications start with an OT assessment — an AHPRA-registered occupational therapist assesses your needs and recommends the works, and complex modifications need a specialist home-modification assessor. We can pass your details to local builders who work alongside OTs.

Can OTs or plan managers request quotes on a participant's behalf?

Yes, and it's often the easiest way to run it. Occupational therapists, support coordinators and plan managers can request a quote directly, and we'll turn it around quickly so it can go into an assessment or report without holding up the plan.

Do you work from an occupational therapist's report?

Yes, and the job is cleaner when there is one. An OT report sets out what the home actually needs to do — transfer space beside the toilet, a shower without a hob, a ramp gradient a wheelchair can genuinely manage — and we scope and price the build against that rather than guessing at it. Where there's no report yet, we can still quote work you already know you need. One thing worth sorting early: whether your funding requires a registered provider depends on how your plan is managed, so confirm that with your plan manager or support coordinator before anything is booked.

OUR PROMISE

What you can expect from us
Nothing structural gets skipped to hit a price

Rail backing, correct shower falls, proper waterproofing and adequate lintels are not the items where a cheaper quote should come from. If our price is higher than another, ask both of us what backing the rails are fixed to and how the shower floor is being graded — the answer is usually the difference.

We say when something will not work

If a specified ramp will not fit the block at a usable gradient, or a bathroom cannot achieve turning space without moving a wall, you will hear it before the quote rather than after the work. That sometimes means telling an OT that a recommendation needs revisiting, which is a normal part of the process and better done early.

The household keeps functioning

People live in these houses while the work happens, and often the person who most needs the bathroom is the one whose bathroom is being rebuilt. We stage the work so there is always something usable, keep dust and disruption contained, and tidy up at the end of each day rather than leaving a site until the job finishes.

WHERE WE WORK

Townsville suburb by suburb

Access work is decided by what the house is, not where it is — and around Townsville the housing type changes markedly from suburb to suburb.

North Ward holds much of the older raised housing, and that makes it the hardest area in Townsville for entry access. A traditional high-set Queenslander can sit well over a metre above ground, which at a usable 1:14 gradient needs seventeen metres of ramp plus landings — more than most inner blocks have available in any direction. Switchback designs solve some of it. Where they do not, a platform lift or moving the accessible entry to a rear or under-house door closer to ground level is often the better outcome, and we will raise that rather than building something technically compliant and practically exhausting.

Kirwan is largely single-storey slab-on-ground housing on flat blocks, which is close to the easiest access situation available. Entry ramps are short or unnecessary, thresholds are low, and level-entry shower conversions are simpler because there is no subfloor to work around. The constraint here is internal rather than external: circulation space inside compact bathrooms and hallways, where the fix is usually a wall or a door swing rather than anything to do with the entry.

Aitkenvale and Annandale sit between those two, with a mix of raised and lowset homes and a good deal of 1970s and 1980s stock. That era brings its own pattern — small bathrooms with the toilet in a separate room, narrow internal doorways, and thresholds between every floor covering. The work here is usually less about the entry and more about the path through the house: getting from a bedroom to a bathroom in a wheelchair often needs two doorways widened and a threshold removed rather than one big change.

Douglas is dominated by the hospital and university precinct, and a share of our work there follows hospital discharge — a house that needs to be made safe on a deadline rather than modified at leisure. Those jobs get staged deliberately: grab rails with proper backing, a handrail at the steps and a temporary modular ramp can be done quickly, while a full level-entry bathroom involves waterproofing and drying time that genuinely cannot be compressed. Telling us the discharge date early changes what we recommend doing first.

HOW IT WORKS

How NDIS home modifications actually get approved and built

The building is the straightforward part. The process around it is what people find confusing, and knowing the shape of it makes the whole thing faster.

Home modifications under the NDIS generally fall into two broad groups, and which one you are in changes how much process is involved. Minor modifications are lower-complexity changes that improve safe access without significant structural work — grab rails, lever tapware, a handrail, a small threshold ramp. More substantial home modifications involve structural change: removing a shower hob and re-grading a floor, widening a load-bearing doorway, building a permanent ramp, reconfiguring a bathroom. The second group requires more assessment, more documentation and usually more waiting, which is worth knowing at the start so the timeline is not a surprise.

The sequence is normally the same. An occupational therapist assesses what the person needs the home to do and documents it — this is the foundation of everything downstream, and it is their professional judgement rather than a builder's. Builder quotes are then obtained against that report, which is where we come in. The quotes and the report go to the NDIA or through the plan manager for approval. Once approved, the work is scheduled and built, and for substantial modifications the OT usually confirms on completion that what was built matches what was recommended.

Two things speed this up more than anything else. The first is an itemised quote. If a quote is a single number, a plan manager cannot match it against the report and an approver cannot see what they are approving — and if funding is granted in stages, an unitemised quote cannot be staged. We break quotes down by element for exactly this reason. The second is flagging conflicts early. If a report specifies something that will not work on the actual site — a ramp gradient the block cannot accommodate, turning space a bathroom cannot achieve without moving a wall — that needs raising before the quote goes in, not after approval, because resolving it afterwards means going back around the loop.

One question we get constantly: whether the builder needs to be a registered NDIS provider. That depends on how the plan is managed rather than on the work itself, and it is genuinely worth confirming with your plan manager or support coordinator before anything is booked. It is a straightforward question with a clear answer for your situation, and it is much better established at the start than discovered at invoicing. We are not in a position to advise on your plan — but we would much rather you ask early than assume.

LOCAL CONDITIONS

Why ramps are hard on a Townsville Queenslander

The single most common disappointment in access work here comes down to arithmetic that nobody does until a builder is standing in the yard.

An accessible ramp is built to a gradient of about 1:14 — one unit of rise for every fourteen of horizontal run. That ratio is not arbitrary. It is roughly the limit at which a person can self-propel a manual wheelchair up a slope without assistance, and steeper ramps become both exhausting to ascend and genuinely dangerous to descend. It also means required length is fixed by the height you are climbing, and nothing about design or materials changes it.

Apply that to Townsville's housing. A lowset home with a 300mm step needs a bit over four metres of ramp — easy on almost any block. A traditional high-set Queenslander with a floor 1.2 metres above ground needs around seventeen metres, and the standard also calls for level landings at intervals along the run and at both ends, adding further length. Very few inner-suburban blocks have seventeen metres of clear run available in a straight line, particularly at the front of the house.

The usual solution is a switchback: the ramp runs, turns on a level landing, and runs back the other way, folding the length into the depth of a yard. Done well this is unobtrusive and works fine. It needs width to turn, though, and on a narrow block it can consume most of a side yard or the entire front garden — which is a real cost to a household even when it is not a financial one.

Where a switchback does not fit, two alternatives deserve serious consideration before anyone compromises the gradient. A platform lift needs a fraction of the footprint and handles a large rise directly, at higher cost and with ongoing maintenance. Or the accessible entry moves: many raised Townsville homes have a rear door, a laundry or an under-house area considerably closer to ground level than the front door, and a short ramp there can be far better than a long one at the front. What should not happen is building at 1:8 because that is what fits — a gradient nobody can self-propel is not access, it is a slope with handrails, and it will not pass an OT's review either.

HOW LONG IT TAKES

Why home modifications take longer than the building work does

Almost all of the elapsed time in a modification project happens before anyone picks up a tool — and knowing that changes how you plan it.

The construction itself is usually the shortest phase. A set of properly backed grab rails is a day. A ramp is days to a week or two depending on length and footings. Even a full level-entry bathroom conversion is measured in weeks, and much of that is waterproofing and tiling that has to cure and cannot be hurried — a bathroom rushed at that stage is one that leaks into the wall cavity later.

What takes the time is everything around it. Getting an occupational therapy assessment scheduled and the report written. Obtaining builder quotes, which requires builders to visit, measure and price. Approval, which for substantial modifications is not immediate. And then scheduling the work into a builder's calendar. Each step is reasonable on its own and they add up to months rather than weeks, particularly for structural work.

There are ways to lose less time. Getting quotes organised promptly once the OT report exists is the obvious one — reports sometimes sit while everyone waits for someone else to act. Itemised quotes prevent a round trip when an approver wants to see the breakdown. Raising site conflicts before submission avoids the worst delay of all, which is approval for something that then turns out to be unbuildable as specified. And if the modification is for a rental, landlord consent should be started early rather than at the end, because it is frequently the item that holds everything up and it is entirely outside both our control and the NDIA's.

Where there is a hard deadline — a hospital discharge is the common one — the sensible approach is to split the work. The high-impact, low-complexity items can genuinely be done quickly: rails with proper backing, a handrail at the entry steps, lever hardware, a temporary modular ramp that can be removed later. The structural work is then planned properly on its own timeline. That is a better outcome than compressing a bathroom conversion into a week and living with the consequences, and it is how we would suggest running it if the dates are tight.

WHAT SETS US APART

Why Bendigo homeowners call us
Nothing leaves before you have said so

Every clearance starts from a list of what has to be found — documents, jewellery, photographs, a particular item promised to a particular person — and that search is completed before a single load goes anywhere. Where it is unclear whether something matters, it goes in a box and we ask rather than deciding for you. Putting something aside costs nothing. Sorted, not skipped

A skip bin is cheaper for us and worse for the estate. Household contents separate into things worth selling, things a local charity will genuinely use, material that belongs with a recycler, and a surprisingly small residue that has to go to landfill. Doing that properly takes time, which is most of what a clearance actually costs — but it means proceeds go back to the estate and usable goods stay in Bendigo rather than in a hole in the ground.

We work to the executor's paperwork

Executors are accountable for the estate's assets, and that includes being able to answer a beneficiary who asks months later what happened to something. Estates are usually sold as-is and cosmetic renovation rarely returns the estate's money — buyers of a deceased estate frequently expect to renovate and have priced it in. Clearing, cleaning and tidying the garden makes a real difference to how a property presents; new benchtops generally do not. We would rather talk you out of work than quote for something we do not think the estate should be paying for.

GETTING STARTED

Our deceased estate cleanouts process

A straightforward path from first enquiry to finished work, planned around your property and the level of work involved.

01
Tell us about the property

We look, then quote in writing

03

04

ABOUT US

Deceased estate clearances across Bendigo

We clear deceased estates in Bendigo and the surrounding towns — houses, units, sheds and the garages that everyone forgets about until the last day. Most of our work comes from executors and the solicitors acting for them, and a good deal of it from families who live interstate and need someone local they can trust to go through a parent's house properly.

The work is mostly sorting, not carrying. A house lived in for decades holds documents that matter, items worth selling, a great deal of perfectly usable household goods, and a fairly small amount of actual rubbish — and none of those are obvious from the doorway. Working through it room by room is slower than filling a skip and it is the entire reason to hire someone rather than hiring a bin.

We also try to be useful about what you should not spend money on. Estates are usually sold as-is, cosmetic renovation rarely returns the money, and an empty, clean house with a tidy garden does most of the work at a fraction of the price. If we think you are about to spend the estate's money on something that will not come back, we will say so.

EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW

Deceased Estate Cleanouts in Bendigo, answered
How much does a deceased estate cleanout cost in Bendigo?

In regional Victoria a deceased estate cleanout typically runs about $800–$5,000 depending on the size of the property and the volume of belongings. Pricing is often based on volume (roughly $75 per cubic metre) or the crew's time ($150–$250 per hour for a lead). Sorting, donations and a pre-sale clean can affect the final figure, so it's worth comparing a couple of local quotes.

What happens to belongings during an estate clearance?

A good clearance works to the family's instructions: heirlooms and documents are set aside, usable furniture and goods are donated to charity or sold, and only the remainder is removed and disposed of. Nothing of value is thrown out without your say-so.

Can the estate or solicitor be invoiced directly?

Yes. We can invoice the estate or the acting solicitor directly, which is usually simpler than a family member paying out of pocket and seeking reimbursement later. Tell us who should receive the invoice when you book and we'll set it up that way from the start.

What happens to everything that leaves the house?

It gets separated rather than skipped. Anything the family has asked us to keep aside is found and set aside first, before a single load goes anywhere. Saleable furniture and household goods go to auction or resale where that's worth doing, and the proceeds belong to the estate. Usable clothing, linen, books and kitchenware go to local charities. Scrap metal and e-waste go to the appropriate recyclers. What genuinely can't be reused goes to landfill last, not first. If you want a record of where things went — and executors frequently do — ask us and we'll keep one.

OUR PROMISE

What you can expect from us
What you asked us to find, we find

The keep list is the first job, not something fitted in around the clearing. If something on it cannot be found, you will hear that from us directly rather than discovering it after the house is empty. And if we come across something that looks like it might matter but is not on the list, it goes aside and we ask you about it.

The estate gets a record

Written documentation of what left the property and where it went — sold, donated, recycled or disposed of. Executors get asked for this, sometimes long afterwards, and it is impossible to reconstruct once the job is finished. You get it whether or not you think you will need it.

We will not rush the family

Some families want the house cleared this week. Others need to walk through it a few times first, and some need to stop halfway and come back. All of that is normal and none of it is a problem. We work at whatever pace you set, across as many visits as it takes, and we will not put pressure on a decision that is not ours to make.

WHERE WE WORK

Bendigo suburb by suburb

What a clearance involves varies more by the kind of property than by the suburb — but around Bendigo those two track each other fairly closely.

Strathdale and Kennington cover much of the established family housing on the eastern side, and the clearances there tend to be the largest. These are homes people stayed in for decades, often with a full garage, a garden shed and a roof space that has been accumulating since the seventies. The sorting takes longer than the removal, and it is where the useful items are most likely to be buried — the roof space and the shed are where documents, tools and things of genuine value most often turn up. Kennington sits closer to the centre, so street access is tighter on some blocks and the removal has to be staged around where a truck can actually park.

Eaglehawk and Golden Square hold a lot of the older cottages, and the pattern is different. The houses themselves are smaller, but the sheds and yards are frequently fuller — workshops, tools, materials kept because they might be useful, and decades of things stored down the side of the house. A cottage clearance that looks modest from the street regularly turns out to be a large job once the outbuildings are opened, which is exactly why we quote after looking rather than from a room count.

Kangaroo Flat spans a wide range, from older houses through to units and townhouses. Unit and retirement-village clearances have their own constraints: access arrangements through a body corporate or village management, lift bookings in some buildings, and restrictions on when a truck can be in the driveway. Those are all workable, but they need arranging in advance rather than discovering on the morning, so it helps to tell us early if the property is one of those.

Across all of it, the two things that change a quote most are how full the property is rather than how big it is, and whether the sheds and garage are included. A large house that has already been partly emptied by family is a smaller job than a small one that has not been touched. If you can tell us roughly which of those you have, the quote will be far closer to the final number.

WHAT IT COSTS

What a deceased estate clearance costs, and what changes the number

Clearances are quoted per property rather than by the load, and the size of the house matters less than most people assume.

The single biggest variable is not floor area — it is how full the property is. A three-bedroom house that has already been partly emptied by family is a materially smaller job than a two-bedroom unit that has not been touched in forty years. When you ask for a quote, a rough sense of how full it is will get you a closer number than the number of bedrooms will. The second variable, and the one most often left out until the last day, is the outbuildings: sheds, garages, carports and under-house storage. A cottage that looks modest from the street can become a large job the moment the shed is opened, which is why we quote after looking rather than over the phone.

The third is how much sorting is needed versus straight removal. Sorting is the labour, and labour is most of the cost. If the family has already been through the house and simply needs the remainder taken away, say so — that is a much smaller job and it should be priced as one. If nobody has been able to face it and everything needs going through carefully, that is the expensive end, and it is also where hiring someone rather than a skip bin actually earns its keep.

Access is the fourth. A unit with lift access and a loading zone, a house with a long driveway, a property on a narrow street where the truck cannot get close — these change how many hours the job takes regardless of volume. Body corporate or retirement village arrangements can add booking constraints too. None of these are problems, but they need to be known in advance rather than discovered on the morning.

Two things work in the other direction. Saleable furniture and household goods can go to auction or resale with proceeds returning to the estate, which offsets part of the cost — though we will be honest that most household contents are worth less at auction than families hope, and we would rather tell you that than let you budget on it. And booking the clearance and the pre-sale clean together is generally cheaper than two contractors, because the property is only attended once and the waste goes in the same loads. Ask for the quote in writing and itemised if the estate's accounts need it.

FOR EXECUTORS

Clearing a house before probate: the shape of the question

This comes up in almost every enquiry, and the honest answer is that it depends on the estate — which is a question for the solicitor, not for us.

The general position is that an executor is responsible for the estate's assets, and the contents of a house are assets. That is why the timing question is not really about the house at all — it is about whether the person instructing the clearance has the authority to deal with the estate's property yet, and that depends on the will, on whether a grant of probate has been made or is needed, and on whether anything about the estate is contested. Plenty of estates are cleared before a grant without any difficulty. Some should wait. We are not in a position to tell you which yours is, and anyone in our trade who confidently tells you otherwise is guessing with your liability.

What we would say is that the question is worth asking the solicitor explicitly rather than assuming, because the cost of asking is a phone call and the cost of getting it wrong falls on the executor personally. If a solicitor is already administering the estate, they will usually have a clear view and will often prefer to instruct the clearance themselves. That is a perfectly normal arrangement and it is one we work with regularly.

There are things you can sensibly do while that is being sorted out. Securing the property matters — an empty house with contents in it is a target, and insurers can be particular about unoccupied properties. Making a list of anything that must be found and kept is useful work at any stage, and it is genuinely easier while family memory is fresh about where things were kept. Photographing rooms before anything moves is worth ten minutes and occasionally settles a question later. And getting a written quote costs nothing and commits you to nothing, so there is no reason to delay that part.

When you are ready to proceed, we take instructions from the executor or from the solicitor acting for the estate, we put the scope in writing, and we invoice the estate directly rather than a family member. If the timing needs to move because probate is taking longer than expected, that is ordinary and we will simply reschedule. Nothing about this work benefits from being rushed, and an estate clearance booked before the authority is settled helps nobody.

THE CONTENTS

What actually happens to a lifetime of belongings

The question families ask most, and the one that decides whether a clearance was done properly or just quickly.

Everything separates into four streams, and the order matters. First is the keep list: anything the family has asked to be found, plus anything we come across that looks like it might matter and was not on the list. That is searched for before a single load leaves, and where we are unsure, it goes in a box and we ask. The cost of setting something aside is nothing; the cost of getting it wrong is permanent, and no discount afterwards makes up for a photograph album in a skip.

Second is anything genuinely saleable. Furniture, collectables, tools, occasionally jewellery or items with real auction value. These go to auction or resale where it is worth doing, and the proceeds belong to the estate. We will give you an honest view on whether there is much there — most household contents are worth considerably less than families expect, and encouraging an estate to budget against imagined auction proceeds does nobody any favours. Where something looks like it may be genuinely valuable and we are not qualified to judge it, we will say so and suggest a valuer rather than guessing.

Third is donation. A large proportion of what comes out of a long-occupied house is perfectly usable: clothing, linen, books, kitchenware, furniture that will not fetch anything at auction but that somebody will be glad of. That goes to local Bendigo charities. Families are almost always pleased to hear it, and it is a substantially better outcome than landfill for goods with years of life left in them. Scrap metal and e-waste go to the appropriate recyclers rather than into general waste.

Landfill is last and it is smaller than people expect. What is left after the other three streams is generally soiled, broken or genuinely worthless. If you want a record of how it broke down — what was sold, what was donated and to whom, what was recycled and what was disposed of — ask, and we will keep one. Why Bendigo homeowners call us
Nothing leaves before you have said so

Every clearance starts from a list of what has to be found — documents, jewellery, photographs, a particular item promised to a particular person — and that search is completed before a single load goes anywhere. Where it is unclear whether something matters, it goes in a box and we ask rather than deciding for you. Putting something aside costs nothing. Getting it wrong cannot be undone, and no apology afterwards is worth anything to the person who wanted it.

Sorted, not skipped

A skip bin is cheaper for us and worse for the estate. Household contents separate into things worth selling, things a local charity will genuinely use, material that belongs with a recycler, and a surprisingly small residue that has to go to landfill. Doing that properly takes time, which is most of what a clearance actually costs — but it means proceeds go back to the estate and usable goods stay in Bendigo rather than in a hole in the ground.

We work to the executor's paperwork

Executors are accountable for the estate's assets, and that includes being able to answer a beneficiary who asks months later what happened to something. So we invoice the estate or the acting solicitor directly rather than putting a family member out of pocket, we keep a written record of where contents went, and we can itemise the invoice by category if the estate's accounts need it. None of that is reconstructable after the fact, which is why it is done as we go.

No judgement on a hard house

Heavily cluttered properties are usually the product of grief, illness or decades of small decisions, and the families dealing with them are often embarrassed on behalf of someone they loved. You do not need to manage that feeling around us. We have done these before, we work discreetly, unmarked arrangements can be made if that matters, and we do not discuss properties we have worked on with anyone.

We will tell you what not to spend money on

Estates are usually sold as-is and cosmetic renovation rarely returns the estate's money — buyers of a deceased estate frequently expect to renovate and have priced it in. Clearing, cleaning and tidying the garden makes a real difference to how a property presents; new benchtops generally do not. We would rather talk you out of work than quote for something we do not think the estate should be paying for.

A straightforward path from first enquiry to finished work, planned around your property and the level of work involved.

Deceased estate clearances across Bendigo

We clear deceased estates in Bendigo and the surrounding towns — houses, units, sheds and the garages that everyone forgets about until the last day. The work is mostly sorting, not carrying. Working through it room by room is slower than filling a skip and it is the entire reason to hire someone rather than hiring a bin.

Deceased Estate Cleanouts in Bendigo, answered
How much does a deceased estate cleanout cost in Bendigo?

In regional Victoria a deceased estate cleanout typically runs about $800–$5,000 depending on the size of the property and the volume of belongings. Pricing is often based on volume (roughly $75 per cubic metre) or the crew's time ($150–$250 per hour for a lead). Can the estate or solicitor be invoiced directly?

What happens to everything that leaves the house?

It gets separated rather than skipped. Anything the family has asked us to keep aside is found and set aside first, before a single load goes anywhere. Saleable furniture and household goods go to auction or resale where that's worth doing, and the proceeds belong to the estate. Usable clothing, linen, books and kitchenware go to local charities. Scrap metal and e-waste go to the appropriate recyclers. What genuinely can't be reused goes to landfill last, not first. If you want a record of where things went — and executors frequently do — ask us and we'll keep one.

OUR PROMISE

What you can expect from us
What you asked us to find, we find

The keep list is the first job, not something fitted in around the clearing. If something on it cannot be found, you will hear that from us directly rather than discovering it after the house is empty. And if we come across something that looks like it might matter but is not on the list, it goes aside and we ask you about it.

The estate gets a record

Written documentation of what left the property and where it went — sold, donated, recycled or disposed of. Executors get asked for this, sometimes long afterwards, and it is impossible to reconstruct once the job is finished. You get it whether or not you think you will need it.

We will not rush the family

Some families want the house cleared this week. Others need to walk through it a few times first, and some need to stop halfway and come back. All of that is normal and none of it is a problem. We work at whatever pace you set, across as many visits as it takes, and we will not put pressure on a decision that is not ours to make.

WHERE WE WORK

Bendigo suburb by suburb

What a clearance involves varies more by the kind of property than by the suburb — but around Bendigo those two track each other fairly closely.

Strathdale and Kennington cover much of the established family housing on the eastern side, and the clearances there tend to be the largest. These are homes people stayed in for decades, often with a full garage, a garden shed and a roof space that has been accumulating since the seventies. The sorting takes longer than the removal, and it is where the useful items are most likely to be buried — the roof space and the shed are where documents, tools and things of genuine value most often turn up. Kennington sits closer to the centre, so street access is tighter on some blocks and the removal has to be staged around where a truck can actually park.

Eaglehawk and Golden Square hold a lot of the older cottages, and the pattern is different. The houses themselves are smaller, but the sheds and yards are frequently fuller — workshops, tools, materials kept because they might be useful, and decades of things stored down the side of the house. A cottage clearance that looks modest from the street regularly turns out to be a large job once the outbuildings are opened, which is exactly why we quote after looking rather than from a room count.

Kangaroo Flat spans a wide range, from older houses through to units and townhouses. Unit and retirement-village clearances have their own constraints: access arrangements through a body corporate or village management, lift bookings in some buildings, and restrictions on when a truck can be in the driveway. Those are all workable, but they need arranging in advance rather than discovering on the morning, so it helps to tell us early if the property is one of those.

Across all of it, the two things that change a quote most are how full the property is rather than how big it is, and whether the sheds and garage are included. A large house that has already been partly emptied by family is a smaller job than a small one that has not been touched. If you can tell us roughly which of those you have, the quote will be far closer to the final number.

WHAT IT COSTS

What a deceased estate clearance costs, and what changes the number

Clearances are quoted per property rather than by the load, and the size of the house matters less than most people assume.

The single biggest variable is not floor area — it is how full the property is. A three-bedroom house that has already been partly emptied by family is a materially smaller job than a two-bedroom unit that has not been touched in forty years. When you ask for a quote, a rough sense of how full it is will get you a closer number than the number of bedrooms will. The second variable, and the one most often left out until the last day, is the outbuildings: sheds, garages, carports and under-house storage. A cottage that looks modest from the street can become a large job the moment the shed is opened, which is why we quote after looking rather than over the phone.

The third is how much sorting is needed versus straight removal. Sorting is the labour, and labour is most of the cost. If the family has already been through the house and simply needs the remainder taken away, say so — that is a much smaller job and it should be priced as one. If nobody has been able to face it and everything needs going through carefully, that is the expensive end, and it is also where hiring someone rather than a skip bin actually earns its keep.

Access is the fourth. A unit with lift access and a loading zone, a house with a long driveway, a property on a narrow street where the truck cannot get close — these change how many hours the job takes regardless of volume. Body corporate or retirement village arrangements can add booking constraints too. None of these are problems, but they need to be known in advance rather than discovered on the morning.

Two things work in the other direction. Saleable furniture and household goods can go to auction or resale with proceeds returning to the estate, which offsets part of the cost — though we will be honest that most household contents are worth less at auction than families hope, and we would rather tell you that than let you budget on it. And booking the clearance and the pre-sale clean together is generally cheaper than two contractors, because the property is only attended once and the waste goes in the same loads. Ask for the quote in writing and itemised if the estate's accounts need it.

FOR EXECUTORS

Clearing a house before probate: the shape of the question

This comes up in almost every enquiry, and the honest answer is that it depends on the estate — which is a question for the solicitor, not for us.

The general position is that an executor is responsible for the estate's assets, and the contents of a house are assets. That is why the timing question is not really about the house at all — it is about whether the person instructing the clearance has the authority to deal with the estate's property yet, and that depends on the will, on whether a grant of probate has been made or is needed, and on whether anything about the estate is contested. Plenty of estates are cleared before a grant without any difficulty. Some should wait. We are not in a position to tell you which yours is, and anyone in our trade who confidently tells you otherwise is guessing with your liability.

What we would say is that the question is worth asking the solicitor explicitly rather than assuming, because the cost of asking is a phone call and the cost of getting it wrong falls on the executor personally. If a solicitor is already administering the estate, they will usually have a clear view and will often prefer to instruct the clearance themselves. That is a perfectly normal arrangement and it is one we work with regularly.

There are things you can sensibly do while that is being sorted out. Securing the property matters — an empty house with contents in it is a target, and insurers can be particular about unoccupied properties. Making a list of anything that must be found and kept is useful work at any stage, and it is genuinely easier while family memory is fresh about where things were kept. Photographing rooms before anything moves is worth ten minutes and occasionally settles a question later. And getting a written quote costs nothing and commits you to nothing, so there is no reason to delay that part.

When you are ready to proceed, we take instructions from the executor or from the solicitor acting for the estate, we put the scope in writing, and we invoice the estate directly rather than a family member. If the timing needs to move because probate is taking longer than expected, that is ordinary and we will simply reschedule. Nothing about this work benefits from being rushed, and an estate clearance booked before the authority is settled helps nobody.

THE CONTENTS

What actually happens to a lifetime of belongings

The question families ask most, and the one that decides whether a clearance was done properly or just quickly.

Everything separates into four streams, and the order matters. First is the keep list: anything the family has asked to be found, plus anything we come across that looks like it might matter and was not on the list. That is searched for before a single load leaves, and where we are unsure, it goes in a box and we ask. The cost of setting something aside is nothing; the cost of getting it wrong is permanent, and no discount afterwards makes up for a photograph album in a skip.

Second is anything genuinely saleable. Furniture, collectables, tools, occasionally jewellery or items with real auction value. These go to auction or resale where it is worth doing, and the proceeds belong to the estate. We will give you an honest view on whether there is much there — most household contents are worth considerably less than families expect, and encouraging an estate to budget against imagined auction proceeds does nobody any favours. Where something looks like it may be genuinely valuable and we are not qualified to judge it, we will say so and suggest a valuer rather than guessing.

Third is donation. A large proportion of what comes out of a long-occupied house is perfectly usable: clothing, linen, books, kitchenware, furniture that will not fetch anything at auction but that somebody will be glad of. That goes to local Bendigo charities. Families are almost always pleased to hear it, and it is a substantially better outcome than landfill for goods with years of life left in them. Scrap metal and e-waste go to the appropriate recyclers rather than into general waste.

Landfill is last and it is smaller than people expect. What is left after the other three streams is generally soiled, broken or genuinely worthless. If you want a record of how it broke down — what was sold, what was donated and to whom, what was recycled and what was disposed of — ask, and we will keep one. mainEntity.name: How much does a mobile mechanic cost in Townsville?

acceptedAnswer.text: Mobile mechanics across Australia typically charge a call-out fee of $50-$100 to cover travel and initial diagnosis, plus labour generally in the $80-$150 per hour range, with parts on top. A completed job commonly lands around $180-$220, a logbook service $180-$500 depending on the vehicle, and a basic oil and filter change $80-$180. There are no fixed industry rates, so pricing varies with urgency, day of the week and job complexity. We quote before we start, so you are not agreeing to an open hourly rate and hoping.

mainEntity.name: Will servicing with a mobile mechanic void my new car warranty?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The ACCC has confirmed that under Australian Consumer Law you are not required to service at an authorised dealer to keep your manufacturer warranty. An independent mechanic can carry out and stamp your logbook service, provided they are appropriately qualified, follow the manufacturer's specifications and service intervals, and use parts suitable for the vehicle - the parts do not need to be genuine branded parts.

mainEntity.name: What can't be done in my driveway?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most servicing, brake work, batteries, alternators, starters, cooling system work, suspension components and diagnostics are routine mobile jobs. What needs a workshop is anything requiring a hoist, a machining lathe or specialised equipment - internal engine and transmission rebuilds, clutch replacement on many vehicles, wheel alignments and rotor machining. We can still diagnose those on site so you know what you are dealing with before committing to a tow.

mainEntity.name: What should I have ready when I call about a breakdown?

acceptedAnswer.text: The make, model and rough year of the car, and exactly what it is doing - whether it cranks but will not fire, clicks once, or is completely dead. That distinction narrows the likely fault before we leave and decides which parts go on the van, which is frequently the difference between fixing it on the first visit and having to come back. Tell us where the car is sitting and whether we can get to it, because a home driveway, an open work carpark and a tight underground bay are three different jobs. If it has been jump-started recently, or it sat unused through a hot week, mention that too - both change what we test first.

The car does not have to move first

The one thing a dead car cannot do is drive to a workshop, which is the whole reason this service exists. Most of what a car needs - servicing, brakes, batteries, alternators, starters, cooling system work and diagnostics - needs hand tools and jack stands rather than a hoist. Doing it where the car already sits removes the tow, the drop-off, the courtesy car and the day off work, and for a no-start it is usually cheaper than the tow alone would have been.

Townsville is hard on cars in ways a southern workshop does not see daily.
